item.text:
Verdict: mostly yes, but uneven and coercive. Putin clearly kept a strong top-down grip on the security state and could force personnel changes, budgetary execution, and selective service-delivery follow-through. The main weakness is institutional depth: the system still showed corruption, opacity, and some hard coordination failures.

That is direct evidence of state-wide coordination and follow-through. | 8B.5; also 8B.3 |

That shows follow-through, but one heavily warped toward war priorities. | 8B.5; also 8B.3 |
| Mixed | [Russia: Nations in Transit 2024](https://freedomhouse.org/country/russia/nations-transit/2024) | Freedom House | 2024 | https://freedomhouse.org/country/russia/nations-transit/2024 | Freedom House says regional governments stayed aligned with the Kremlin and Putin directed the cabinet to improve municipal finances, but it also says municipalities lacked financial independence and decisions were made by a small closed circle. This supports strong central control with weak institutional depth. | 8B.5 |

Search gap: I did not find a public, independent, whole-of-government performance audit that tracks execution across all ministries, regions, and agencies in 2024. The strongest evidence is concentrated in defence, security, and a few targeted administrative programs; civilian follow-through is mostly visible through isolated decrees and Reuters reporting rather than a transparent monitoring system.
